title: Another Blow For Bonds?
text:
Another Blow For Bonds?

Tan Kai Xian

Gavekal Research | 24 Sep 2026

Propelled by much stronger-than-expected PMI readings and a rebound in the price of oil, the 10-year US treasury yield jumped 18bp Wednesday, breaking through the 5% level to hit 5.11%, its highest since the outbreak of the credit crunch in July 2007. With inflation pressure persistent and the US Federal Reserve on a tightening track, few market participants would dismiss the possibility of a further near-term rise in yields. In addition, there is another force that may emerge to exert upward pressure on yields: there are growing signs that the US labor market may be set to tighten, pushing both wage growth and inflation higher.The US labor market has been largely quiescent in recent months. Sure, payrolls jumped by a surprisingly strong 162,000 in August. But payrolls is a volatile series, subject to heavy revision. The three-month moving average of payrolls growth is at 71,000, comfortably within its currently estimated breakeven range of 15,000-87,000: the monthly growth needed to absorb entrants to the labor market and keep the unemployment rate stable.
